summary:
Quinn (Kwindla Hultman Kramer), co-founder of Daily, presents on building enterprise voice AI agents using Pipecat, an open-source, vendor-neutral framework. Daily has built global real-time audio, video, and AI infrastructure since 2016. The talk covers three pillars: writing agent code, deploying it, and connecting users via network or telephony. User expectations are demanding: agents must understand speech, feel conversational, access knowledge bases, sound natural, and respond fast. Humans expect ~500ms conversational response; Quinn recommends targeting 800ms voice-to-voice, with P95 above 800-1000ms for the entire response chain being problematic. Turn detection remains a hard challenge. Developers use Pipecat for battle-tested implementations of turn detection, interruption handling, context management, and asynchronous function calling. Pipecat is 100% open source and vendor neutral, supporting 60+ models and services with client SDKs for JavaScript, React, iOS, and Android. Pipelines are Python-based programmable media elements ranging from simple 3-element setups to complex enterprise integrations.

Deployment is uniquely hard for voice AI: long-running sessions need low-latency protocols, autoscaling isn't available out of the box, and the entire networking stack must be optimized for real time. Pipecat Cloud addresses this as a thin Docker/Kubernetes wrapper optimized for voice AI. Additional features include the open-source smart turn model (hosted free by Fal), Crisp background noise removal (available free in Pipecat Cloud), and native logging/observability building blocks. Background noise is a significant problem because LLMs aren't as resilient as transcription models to noisy environments.

The Q&A covers geographic deployment strategies (deploying close to inference servers for one long-haul trip plus short local trips, or using open weights models locally; Daily's global POPs and private AWS/OCI backbones), speech-to-speech model architectures (Moshi's bidirectional streaming with back-channeling but too small for production; Sesame using Moshi's Mimi encoder; Ultravox on Llama 3 70B), and vendor comparisons. GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash are roughly equivalent in text mode, but Gemini is ~10x cheaper per 30-minute conversation and has superior native audio input support. Speech-to-speech models excel at conversational naturalness but lag in instruction following and function calling reliability. Quinn expects them to become the default for ~95% of voice AI within two years. He elaborates that speech-to-speech models preserve information lost in transcription (e.g., mixed-language input) and may offer lower latency through single inference calls, but audio tokens expand context massively and degrade performance. Insufficient audio training data causes issues like models responding in wrong languages. Big labs will eventually fix these problems because audio and multi-turn conversations matter.

sections.title: Introduction and Daily Background
sections.summary: Quinn introduces himself as co-founder of Daily, stepping in for colleague Mark. Daily has provided global real-time audio, video, and AI infrastructure since 2016. Pipecat sits higher in the stack than Daily's traditional infrastructure business. The talk covers building reliable voice AI agents with open source software and briefly mentions Pipecat Cloud.

sections.title: Voice Agent Fundamentals and User Expectations
sections.summary: Building a voice agent involves writing code, deploying it, and connecting users. User expectations are high: agents must understand speech, feel conversational, connect to knowledge bases, and sound natural. Humans expect ~500ms response times; target 800ms for voice-to-voice. Turn detection—knowing when to respond—remains a hard challenge that AI is improving on but hasn't mastered.

sections.title: Why Use Pipecat Framework
sections.summary: Developers use Pipecat for battle-tested implementations of turn detection, interruption handling, context management, and asynchronous function calling. Pipecat is 100% open source and vendor neutral, supporting multiple telephony providers (Twilio, Pivo), an open-source audio smart turn model, and 60+ models and services. Client SDKs exist for JavaScript, React, iOS, and Android for multimodal applications.

sections.title: Pipecat Pipeline Architecture
sections.summary: Pipecat agents are pipelines of programmable media handling elements written in Python. They range from simple 3-element pipelines to complex enterprise integrations. Examples include OpenAI audio models (chained transcription+LLM+TTS vs speech-to-speech, switchable in 3-4 lines) and a Gemini multimodal game using two API instances with an LLM-as-judge pattern, selectively routing audio frames through both pipelines.

sections.title: Deployment Challenges and Pipecat Cloud
sections.summary: Voice AI deployment is uniquely hard: long-running sessions need low-latency protocols, and autoscaling isn't available out of the box. Discord questions revealed developers struggled with Kubernetes. Pipecat Cloud is a thin Docker/Kubernetes wrapper optimized for voice AI, addressing fast cold starts (critical when users call and expect immediate pickup), autoscaling for unpredictable traffic, and the fundamental difference between real-time conversational latency and HTTP workloads.

sections.title: Latency Optimization, Noise Handling, and Observability
sections.summary: Quinn details how P95 latency above 800-1000ms for the entire voice-to-voice chain is problematic, requiring every inference call to be much faster. Global deployment, GDPR/data residency, and cost optimization all matter. Turn detection is a top-3 2025 problem; Pipecat's open-source smart turn model runs free in Pipecat Cloud (hosted by Fal). Background noise is a significant issue—transcription models are resilient but LLMs aren't, causing spurious interruptions. Crisp offers the best commercial noise removal, available free in Pipecat Cloud. Native logging and observability building blocks are exposed through Pipecat Cloud and partner integrations.

sections.title: Q&A: Geographic Deployment, Speech-to-Speech Models, and Vendor Comparison
sections.summary: Q&A covers geographic deployment (for users far from inference servers like Australia: deploy close to inference servers for one long-haul plus short trips, or use open weights models locally; Daily has global POPs and private AWS/OCI backbones). On speech-to-speech models: Moshi (Kyutai) uses bidirectional streaming enabling back-channeling but is too small for production; Sesame uses Moshi's Mimi encoder but isn't fully released; Ultravox on Llama 3 70B is worth trying. Large-lab speech-to-speech models (OpenAI GPT-4 audio, Gemini 2.0 Flash audio) excel at naturalness but lag in instruction following. GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash are roughly equivalent in text mode, but Gemini is ~10x cheaper with better native audio input. Quinn expects speech-to-speech to become default for ~95% of voice AI within two years.

sections.title: Q&A: Speech-to-Speech vs Transcription Trade-offs
sections.summary: Quinn elaborates on practical and philosophical reasons for choosing speech-to-speech models. Practically, transcription loses information—mixed-language input is very hard for small transcription models, so routing audio directly to a large LLM with broad language knowledge is advantageous. Speech-to-speech may also offer lower latency through a single inference call rather than chained calls, though today this depends more on APIs and inference stacks than model architecture. Philosophically, audio tokens expand context massively relative to text, degrading model performance. Nobody has as much audio training data as text, so transfer learning from text to audio is imperfect—audio-to-audio models sometimes respond in totally different languages because latent space projections from audio differ from text even for identical content. Big labs will fix these issues over time because audio and multi-turn conversations matter.

Showed Python code and flow diagram for a Gemini multimodal live API game using two instances—one for conversation, one as game participant with LLM-as-judge pattern
